title: Deployments as Controlled Experiments

sections.title: Release Gates for Replica Read Routing

html:
Every limit in Chapter 9 was a measured number, and every measured number describes the code that was running when someone measured it. Change the code, and the number may stop being true. That is why the apps on your phone rarely change for everyone on the same day. An update often installs with nothing visible, and days later a feature appears because the team has switched it on for your account. Engineers use the same separation in production. They deploy a version, confirm that it runs, and only then expose a new code path to a rising share of traffic while they watch what it does.

Baodium’s Recommendation Service team learned why that separation matters a few months after the connection-pool incident. An engineer rewrote a database query. The new version returned the same recommendations, ran faster in an isolated benchmark, and passed its functional tests, so the team released it through an ordinary rolling deployment.

Under production traffic, the new query occupied its connections longer, and product pages began waiting for connections again. Kubernetes reported every instance as healthy, because the readiness checks only confirmed that each instance had started. Nothing in the rollout compared connection use between the old and new versions before replacing the next instance. The engineers rolled back, and then sat down to redesign the release process itself, starting with how much traffic a canary would need before its measurements could justify going further.

Release Hypothesis and Failure Risk

Before releasing the recommendation query, Baodium’s engineers expected faster database execution without additional connection occupancy. That was the claim the canary had to test under concurrent production traffic. If acquisition waits rose despite faster SQL execution, the release would stop until the cause was understood. Writing down both the expected improvement and the stop condition focused the review on evidence from the actual request path.

CPU utilization would reveal little about this regression because the queries were acquiring database connections for longer. The release gates therefore included connection occupancy, acquisition latency, query execution, recommendation delivery, and product-page response time.

The revised query occupied connections longer under concurrent traffic. Although its isolated benchmark was faster, Recommendation Service now had less room for bursts in the same 40-connection pool. Acquisition latency rose as the release reached more customers. Chapter 2 already established how to estimate that demand, so the release review concentrated on verifying it under representative concurrency. The engineers reproduced the regression using concurrent queries with representative parameters and traced it to an index choice that performed well in isolation but poorly under contention.

Other releases call for other hypotheses, about memory allocation, backend calls per request, event volume, or response correctness. In each case, the plan names the observation the team expects and the regression that would stop the rollout.

Deployment Strategy and Feature Exposure

Installing new code and exposing users to it are separate steps, and separating them gives the team more control. A team can install a binary with the new query path disabled, verify that it starts and is compatible, and then enable the path for selected requests. Alternatively, the router can send a fraction of requests to instances that run the new binary. These choices decide what the team can reverse and how much processing the change can affect before anyone notices a problem. Table Table summarizes the common mechanisms.

These mechanisms can be combined. A blue-green setup can send a weighted share of traffic to the new environment as a canary before the full switch, a rolling update can pause between steps for evaluation, and a feature flag can restrict new behavior further inside the new version. The right combination depends on what the release is testing. A query regression needs representative database work, a new response format needs every consumer to be compatible with it, and a memory leak needs an observation period long enough for retained memory to reach a measurable level.

Rolling Updates

A rolling update suits services whose old and new instances can serve traffic side by side. Chapter 6 showed the Kubernetes policy that adds one surge instance at a time and never removes an old instance until its replacement is ready. Figure Figure steps through one replacement.

The readiness check did not catch the slow query because readiness shows only that an instance is prepared to accept requests. A new instance can pass it and then run a far more expensive query once production traffic arrives, as happened with the recommendation release. A plain rolling update needs an additional release policy whenever promotion should depend on performance. Similarly, the Deployment’s progress deadline reports a rollout that has stalled, but it does not roll anything back, so automatic restoration needs a controller or an operating procedure that takes that action. And as Chapter 2 explained, the database still has to accommodate every live process during the rollout, including instances that are draining.

Blue-Green Environments

Blue-green deployment maintains two complete environments, one serving users, called blue, and one idle, called green. Think of a theater with two stages, where the next show is set up on the second stage while the current one plays, and the audience changes stages only when everything is ready. The team installs the new release in green, tests it there without any production traffic, and then switches the router so that new requests go to green, as Figure Figure shows. Because blue is still ready to serve, switching back is a routing change rather than an instance-by-instance replacement, which can make restoration much faster.

Several details limit that advantage. Connections and requests that started before the switch can continue on the old environment afterward, and an environment that has been idle may need warming before it can accept the full request rate. Both environments may also run connection pools, background workers, and scheduled tasks, so Baodium’s cutover plan covers those processes as well, because starting a second environment must not create a second active scheduler or double the background workload. Most important, the two environments usually share a database, and a new version that writes data the old version cannot read can make blue unusable even though its processes are healthy. You will come back to that problem later in the chapter.

Field note

Cloudflare, July 2019

Cloudflare’s postmortem attributes its July 2, 2019 outage to a new rule for its web application firewall. The rule contained a regular expression that could backtrack catastrophically, and on machines across the network it used so much processor time that customers received errors for 27 minutes. Firewall rules were deployed to the whole network within seconds, because emergency rules against new attacks need to take effect everywhere at once, and as a result an ordinary rule change bypassed the gradual rollout that most of Cloudflare’s software went through. Cloudflare restored traffic by disabling the managed firewall rules globally, then fixed the rule and re-enabled the firewall.

A rule that executes is code, and it needs a canary, a comparison against a concurrent baseline, and a way to stop it, just as a binary does. The recovery also depended on a control that disabled the rules across the entire network, which existed before the incident and worked during it.

Source: original published account.

Canary Cohort Sizing

When the team re-released the corrected query, it used a canary. The name comes from the canaries coal miners once carried underground, which showed signs of danger before the miners did. A canary release limits the first exposure to a small share of production traffic while the team compares the new version with the stable one. Figure Figure shows the decision the canary exists to support.

The stable version provides a concurrent comparison. The canary needs a similar request mix, because lower traffic or easier requests can make a new build appear faster without improving customer latency.

Suppose Recommendation Service runs 20 instances, each receiving about 400 lookups per second, for a fleet total of about 8,000. Routing 5 percent of requests to one canary instance gives it about 400 lookups per second, and the other 19 instances share the other 95 percent at about the same rate each. The canary experiences the same per-instance load as the stable instances, which is the condition under which the original regression appeared.

Canary size is a trade-off between exposure and evidence. A small canary affects few users but may collect too few requests for a stable estimate of a high percentile, while a larger canary collects evidence faster at the cost of exposing more users. Five percent is a starting point, and the team supplements it with early signals, such as connection acquisition time, that respond to a regression well before a high percentile can be estimated reliably.

Now suppose the team spread the same 5 percent across five canary instances instead of one. Each would receive only about 80 lookups per second, and at that rate the new query might show no acquisition delay at all, even though it would create contention at the normal rate of 400. The routing weight and the number of canary instances have to be chosen together. The router controls the traffic weight independently of the number of instances, and the release dashboard reports the rate each instance receives, because a configured percentage is only a request to the router, and the comparison depends on the measured rate.

Cohort Selection

Request rate is only one part of a fair comparison. Region, catalog size, query parameters, cache state, and user behavior all affect resource use, so a canary that happens to serve mostly small catalogs can seem faster than a stable population serving large ones. An internal-user cohort, sometimes called dogfooding, is useful for functional feedback but says little about production performance. For the query release, Baodium used a production cohort in which every relevant request class was represented, compared the known cost categories between the two populations, and inspected instances individually whenever fleet averages hid an imbalance.

Assigning each customer permanently to one version stops a customer from switching versions in the middle of an interaction. It also means that a small share of customers may not produce the same share of requests, so the release record includes both the assignment and the observed request volume. A single canary instance can also be affected by its node or placement. When its measurements are unusual and the cause is unclear, the team repeats the comparison on another placement before blaming the query, and exposure does not increase while that investigation is open.

Startup and Warm State

A new instance opens connections, loads metadata, and fills its local caches as its first requests arrive. Those costs are part of the deployment’s behavior, so they need their own observation rather than being excluded from the result. As Chapter 6 described, if an instance cannot serve normal traffic until it has finished preparing, either its readiness check must wait for that preparation or the router must increase its traffic gradually. A fixed delay after startup helps only when testing has shown what happens during that delay, because five uneventful minutes may mean only that a rarely used path has not run yet and a large cache is still empty.

Shared Dependencies

Canary and stable instances usually share a database, and that creates the canary’s main blind spot. An expensive canary query can raise database CPU or contention until both populations slow down, and when both slow down together, the gap between them shrinks, so a harmful change can pass as harmless. It is like a clinical trial in which the new drug contaminates the water supply that the control group also drinks. A small difference between canary and stable response times is not evidence that a release is acceptable, because both may have deteriorated. Baodium compares the two versions and also checks absolute limits on user-facing latency and shared resources. The traffic percentage limits how many requests reach the canary directly, but a shared dependency can spread the consequences to every request.

Shadow testing, in which copies of production reads are sent to the new version and the responses discarded, has the same property. The copied reads use actual backend capacity even though no customer ever sees their results, so shadow traffic needs its own allowance. Requests that change state must either run in isolation or have their effects suppressed, which in turn limits what the test can prove.

Decision review

Promote or pause?

Recommendation Service has 20 instances, each handling about 400 lookups per second. The canary is one instance at 5 percent exposure. After twenty minutes it shows page p99 at 231 ms against a baseline of 220 ms, no errors, and mean connection occupancy of 74 ms against a baseline of 70 ms. The release owner wants to go to 25 percent.

Promote. An 11-millisecond difference at the p99 is within ordinary variation, and there are no errors.

Pause. The occupancy difference is small but consistent, and it is the measurement that scales with exposure.

Promote, but only to 10 percent, and re-evaluate.

In twenty minutes, the canary handles about 400 lookups per second for 1,200 seconds, or 480,000 lookups, so with complete recording, about 4,800 of them fall in the slowest one percent. That is a substantial sample, but its duration, request mix, and the dependence between successive requests all affect the comparison, and neither the mean nor the p99 difference alone proves a regression.

The occupancy difference means 400×0.004=1.6400 \times 0.004 = 1.6400×0.004=1.6 more connections in use on the canary instance. If the same rate and difference applied to all 20 instances, full promotion would add about 32 connections across the fleet, although shared-database contention could change those durations, so the estimate needs testing.

Under B, the team pauses promotion and compares the observations with the release gate written before the rollout, checking that the workloads match. The gate in the next section allows an occupancy difference of up to 5 ms, so a consistent 4 ms passes, and the gate then permits promotion. C is reasonable only if the evaluation plan already calls for a bounded intermediate step with defined stop criteria. A assumes that the variation is acceptable without making that comparison.

Evaluation Gates

A gate records, before the release begins, the evidence required before exposure increases. Writing it in advance matters because a team looking at a promising canary is inclined to explain away an inconvenient number, whereas a criterion recorded beforehand cannot be adjusted to fit the result. Scientists call the same safeguard preregistration.

For the recommendation change, connection occupancy was the most direct early measurement, and it had to be compared per version. At 5 percent exposure, a 15-millisecond increase on the canary raises the fleet-wide mean by only 0.75 milliseconds, assuming comparable requests and no secondary effects, which disappears into the noise of a combined average. A version-specific comparison preserves the full 15 milliseconds. The gate also checks acquisition failures and the user-facing page, so that an improved average cannot hide requests that failed or were never completed.

Each evaluation leads to one of three outcomes.

Promote.

The required evidence is present, comparable, and satisfies the recorded criteria.

Pause.

Exposure is frozen at its current level while the team resolves missing evidence, an insufficient sample, or an unexplained difference.

Abort.

New exposure to the candidate is removed through the tested restoration procedure.

A pause leaves the current canary population exposed, so it is the wrong response when that population is experiencing an unacceptable failure. In that case, the right outcome is an abort.

Release Stages and Stop Conditions

Listing Listing shows the level of detail that makes the query release reviewable. The values are specific to this case, and each one needs validation against ordinary variation and the product’s objectives.

The sample requirement sits next to the elapsed interval because elapsed time alone says nothing about how many requests the canary served. The controller checks how many lookups the canary completed, so an interval in which the canary received too little traffic does not pass. The occupancy margin is a small fraction of the original regression, so a repeat of that regression would fail this gate in the first interval, and the absolute limit on acquisition time prevents promotion when both versions are already suffering from serious pool contention.

Two further rules sit outside the performance criteria. User-facing failures and incorrect data trigger an immediate abort, because the controller should not wait two five-minute intervals while requests are returning wrong results. The complete policy also names the person responsible for resolving a pause and a maximum duration for each stage, so that a canary waiting for a signal that never arrives does not run unattended indefinitely.

Deriving the Gate Values

Gate values should never be copied from another service. Each one comes from a short chain of reasoning that another team can repeat with its own measurements, and the chain has five links.

Baseline variation.

The team first looked at two weeks of stable data to see how much occupancy varied on an ordinary day. A threshold smaller than that ordinary wobble would fail healthy releases, so the gate had to sit comfortably above it.

Smallest regression to stop.

Next, the team asked how much extra occupancy the pool could tolerate before bursts started filling it regularly. That operational figure set the threshold. It was a fraction of the original regression, so a repeat of that mistake would fail the gate in its first interval.

Minimum sample.

A comparison needs enough completed requests for the difference to be genuine rather than noise. Averages settle after a few thousand requests, but rare events need far more. Telling a 0.2 percent error rate apart from 0.1 percent takes tens of thousands of requests in each version, which is why error-rate gates need far more traffic than latency gates.

Exposure while waiting.

Every minute spent collecting evidence is a minute in which some customers use the candidate. The team accepted that exposure because the risk under test slowed pages rather than returning wrong data, and correctness failures triggered an immediate abort.

Interval.

Finally, the interval had to deliver the minimum sample even if the canary received only half its expected traffic, and two separate intervals had to produce the same verdict, so one unusual swing could not decide the outcome.

A release with a different risk needs its own chain. A change that affects rare request types needs a larger sample or a targeted test, and a change that could corrupt data needs a much smaller first exposure, however long the evidence then takes to collect.

Observation Windows

The intervals in the release plan do not overlap for a specific reason. Two evaluations of a rolling five-minute window taken one minute apart share four minutes of observations, so treating them as two passes would use the same requests twice. Nonoverlapping intervals avoid that, although production measurements are still correlated from one interval to the next.

The size of a sample also depends on the event being measured. Hundreds of thousands of successful lookups give useful evidence about mean occupancy but say almost nothing about a failure that occurs once per million requests, which needs a targeted test or a broader observation plan. Some risks depend on elapsed time rather than request volume, such as token refresh, scheduled work, cache expiry, and gradual memory growth, and those need observation periods long enough to include them. The release owner chooses the interval to match the suspected failure and records which conditions the canary has not yet exercised.

Version-Labeled Release Telemetry

The release dashboard pairs each instance’s request rate with its connection occupancy, acquisition time, active connections, recommendation delivery, and page outcomes. Cohort percentiles are calculated from the combined histogram observations rather than by averaging per-instance percentiles, for the reasons explained in Chapter 8. Attempted and refused requests are shown next to completed ones, because a version that rejects expensive work could otherwise seem faster by leaving that work out of its completion times.

Each stage decision records the deployed artifact and configuration, the routing weight, the sample interval, the observed values, the thresholds, and the action taken. With that record, an engineer can later explain why exposure increased or why restoration began.

Automated Gates With Argo Rollouts

You do not have to run these evaluations by hand. Progressive-delivery controllers for Kubernetes, such as Argo Rollouts and Flagger, replace the plain Deployment with a resource that advances through canary steps, queries your metrics between them, and promotes or aborts on the result. Listing Listing shows the recommendation release expressed as an Argo Rollout.

Notice the pairing of setCanaryScale and setWeight. It expresses the point from earlier in this chapter that the traffic weight and the number of canary instances must be chosen together. One canary instance receives 5 percent of traffic, and three receive 15 percent, so each canary instance always receives about 400 lookups per second. This works only with a traffic router, here an Istio virtual service. Without one, a controller can approximate a weight only by changing the ratio of canary to stable instances, which ties the two numbers back together.

The gate itself is an analysis template that runs Prometheus queries and compares the results with the thresholds from Listing Listing.

The queries reuse the occupancy histogram from Chapter 1, labeled by version. The five-minute initial delay and five-minute interval produce two nonoverlapping five-minute windows, as the release plan requires, and a failed measurement aborts the rollout and returns traffic to the stable version. The acquisition p99 limit and the absolute user-facing checks are added as further metrics in the same way. You still choose every one of these numbers yourself. It only makes sure that the numbers you derived are applied every time, a check the original rolling update lacked.

Multi-Stage Canary Promotion

A clean result at 5 percent is encouraging, but it does not predict the change’s effect at full exposure. The canary tests the new version only under its own share of traffic, and some costs increase with total exposure. A query can fit comfortably within the database’s CPU when one instance runs it and create contention when all 20 do, and a new cache namespace can produce more misses as each additional caller adopts it. Before treating a canary result as a capacity check, the team reviews the additional shared-resource demand expected at full exposure.

Baodium advances through several stages while preserving representative per-instance traffic, as the Rollout above does. In the 20-instance fleet, a 15-percent stage assigns three instances to the candidate and 17 to the stable version, and each stage repeats the applicable checks, including the absolute database and user-facing measurements, because evidence from one stage applies only to its own level of exposure.

Restoration takes longer as the rollout advances. At the first stage, most instances already run the previous version, whereas near the end, restoring the old version may mean starting or replacing most of the fleet, so the plan allows for that time and for the load on the other instances while it happens. The final stage includes an observation period after full activation. With no stable cohort left for comparison, the evidence at that point comes from absolute limits, earlier comparisons, and per-request-class measurements.

Feature Flags and Runtime Activation

For the recommendation query, a feature flag could have separated installation from activation. Both query paths would be deployed in the same binary, and configuration would select a path for each request, much like a light switch installed during construction but left off until the room is ready. The flag allows the team to disable the new request path during an incident without deploying another image. The cost is an additional code path and an additional configuration state, so every flag needs an owner and a condition for its removal. As the Knight Capital field note below shows, an obsolete activation path can cause a failure years after its original purpose has passed.

Teams often use a feature-management service such as LaunchDarkly, Unleash, or Flagsmith. OpenFeature provides a common interface for applications using different providers. A release owner publishes the flag and its exposure percentage, and the application evaluates the latest configuration available to that instance.

For instance, the first Baodium rollout could publish the values in the listing below.

recommendations_enabled: true
recommendations_exposure_percent: 1
recommendations_revision: 17

The handler would check recommendations_enabled, then choose the new path only when the request belonged to the permitted exposure cohort. The next example illustrates stable cohort assignment without requiring a particular vendor’s SDK:

import hashlib

def in_cohort(customer_id, flag_name, percent):
    key = f"{flag_name}:{customer_id}".encode()
    value = int.from_bytes(hashlib.sha256(key).digest()[:4], "big")
    return value % 10_000 < round(percent * 100)

The same customer receives the same result on each instance, as long as the flag name and percentage are unchanged. A one-percent user cohort may generate more or less than one percent of traffic if customers have different activity levels.1 During Baodium’s incident, the release owner could set exposure to zero in the management console. We would verify when each instance received the new revision and whether any existing request was already executing the recommendation path. The selected variant should be recorded with request telemetry, so we can compare behavior within the same binary.

During a configuration-service outage, an instance may continue using its last cached revision. Baodium’s rollback procedure therefore checked which revision each instance had loaded, including after a network failure. Calls already running on the recommendation path might also require cancellation or time to finish.

A release flag is retired once validation and the restoration period are complete. A later deployment removes the old path, and the flag record is deleted once no deployed version depends on it. Operational switches that are permanent need an owner and regular testing of the fallback they control.

Field note

Knight Capital, August 2012

The order issued by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) against Knight Capital describes a deployment of new trading software to eight servers. The code was installed over several days, and a technician failed to copy it to one of the eight. No second person reviewed the deployment, and no written procedure required one. The new code reused a flag that had once activated an old, long-retired function called Power Peg, and that old code was still present on the eighth server. When orders carrying the reused flag arrived on August 1, seven servers worked correctly and the eighth began sending orders it should never have sent. The SEC reported more than four million executions in about 45 minutes and a loss exceeding $460 million.

During the incident, engineers removed the new code from the seven servers where it had been installed correctly. That made the situation worse, because orders with the flag then reached the old code on every server.

The failure exposed four release requirements. A deployment must be verified on every target, dead code should be removed rather than reactivated through a reused switch, rollback is a change in its own right and needs rehearsal, and a system needs a way to stop that does not depend on the code being stopped.

Source: original published account.

Rollback and Data Compatibility

The recommendation query could be rolled back freely because it did not change any stored data. Chapter 6 raised a concern that matters much more for releases that do. What would the old version do with data the new version has written? Suppose the catalog team wants to replace a category field with category_v2 to support a revised catalog feature. If new readers are deployed while some writers still update only category, those readers return outdated values. If new writers are rolled back after updating only category_v2, the restored readers miss the new data. The way out is a staged compatibility release.

Expansion and Compatible Writers

Safe data changes use an expand-then-contract order, which resembles replacing a road bridge. Engineers build the new bridge beside the old one, open it while the old bridge is still in service, divert traffic gradually, and close the old bridge only when nothing depends on it. In a schema change, the first release adds the new field while existing readers still use the old one.

That schema change needs its own assessment of locking and resource use before it runs. In PostgreSQL, adding a nullable column, or one with a constant default, changes only the table’s metadata and finishes in milliseconds, but the statement still needs a brief exclusive lock on the table. If a long-running transaction is using the table, the ALTER TABLE waits for it, and every query that arrives after the ALTER TABLE waits behind it, so a migration that should take milliseconds can stall the whole table. Setting a short lock_timeout before the migration makes it give up after a short wait and retry instead of blocking the table. Indexes on large tables are built with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY for the same reason. Migration tools such as Flyway, Liquibase, and Alembic run these steps in order and record which ones have been applied, but deciding what is safe to run against a busy table is still your job.

A compatibility release then writes both representations in the same database transaction. The deployment inventory includes background jobs, administrative tools, and recovery workers, because any of them may update the affected records, and before new readers are enabled, the team confirms that every active writer maintains both fields. The compatibility release becomes the approved rollback target for this period, and choosing any earlier release instead would cause damage. Rolling back to an earlier writer that updates only the old field would silently invalidate the new field for every process that has started reading it.

Backfill and Verification

Existing rows are converted in limited batches whose rate is controlled separately from the application deployment, because the backfill competes with ordinary requests for database execution, locks, and I/O. It also produces WAL that every replica has to replay, so Baodium paced its backfill against the replica lag measurements from Chapter 7 and paused it whenever lag rose above the read-routing threshold. Concurrent updates need a defined ordering rule, so that the backfill never overwrites a recently written value with an older copy of the source. The backfill can calculate the new value from the current row under appropriate transaction protection, or it can make each update conditional on the source version it read and retry on conflict.

Verification checks the relationship between the two representations. Checking that the new field is filled in shows only that values exist, not that they are current or correctly converted, so the check compares each converted value with its source. After verification, the team enables new readers progressively, and both representations continue to be maintained for the agreed rollback period.

Contraction

Stopping writes to the old field, or dropping it, ends compatibility with every version that depends on it, so that step happens in a separate release after the earlier rollback target has been retired. The check includes processes that run infrequently, because a monthly report or a recovery tool can depend on the old field long after the serving fleet has upgraded.

Dual writing also has a limit. If the new representation permits values that the old one cannot express, writing both fields cannot make the change reversible, and rollback then requires a deliberate restriction on new values, a conversion, or a plan to repair forward instead.

API and Event Compatibility

The same reasoning applies to interfaces, with one complication. Some consumers of an API are deployed by other teams, or by customers, on their own schedules, and the provider cannot upgrade them as part of its own release, so compatibility rules must cover clients that have not upgraded yet. A mobile app is the extreme case, because some users never update, and a server change can break a version that is still installed on millions of phones.

Adding a field to a response is compatible only with consumers that accept unknown fields. Renaming a field, adding an unexpected enum value, or changing the meaning of an existing value can break a consumer even though the HTTP status is unchanged. For a field replacement, the provider publishes both forms while consumers adopt the new one, and deployment data establishes which consumer versions are still active. Contract tests verify the documented consumer requirements. With a tool such as Pact, each consumer publishes the requests it makes and the response fields it relies on, and the provider’s build fails if a change would break any of them.

Events extend the overlap further, because an upgraded consumer may receive older events from a backlog, a retry queue, or a replay, and an older consumer restored during a rollback may receive events produced by the newer version. A schema registry can enforce part of this. The Confluent Schema Registry, for example, can reject a new event schema that older consumers could not read. The compatibility policy still has to cover retained messages and recovery procedures as well as the versions currently serving requests, and Chapter 12 covers delivery and replay in detail.

Rollback and Restoration Procedure

A restoration test is meaningful only after the candidate has served requests and produced the kinds of state you expect during the release. A rollback rehearsed on a fresh environment leaves out the case that fails in production, in which the new version has already written data that the old version has never read.

For the query change, the procedure begins with the release controller stopping promotion and redirecting new requests to the approved stable path. The application then completes or cancels candidate work according to each request’s contract, and engineers confirm which version is receiving requests and whether the resource measurements are recovering. An earlier image digest is only one part of that procedure, because the matching configuration, compatible credentials, routing policy, and enough serving capacity must all be available too.

Rolling back sometimes takes a while to bring relief. Database work already submitted can continue after the switch, and backlogs, lock contention, or cache entries left by the candidate can delay recovery. When measurements fail to improve, the responder investigates those effects instead of repeating the rollback command. For a release that changes state, restoration also identifies accepted work that needs recovery or correction, because returning to the earlier binary does not undo events already emitted or external operations already performed. The release record distinguishes the time required to stop routing new requests to the candidate from the time required to restore customer-facing service. Those intervals can differ when old requests, database locks, or queued operations continue after rollback.

Release Gates for Replica Read Routing

Some releases put correctness at risk as well as cost. A release that sends account reads to a replica instead of the primary, as Chapter 7 described, can reduce primary load while allowing stale reads, so a gate based only on latency would pass a broken release. Its hypothesis has to name the freshness rule as well. Primary read demand falls without stale reads exceeding the agreed allowance and without missing the latency objective. The evidence then includes read routing, replica lag, fallback frequency to the primary, and request outcomes. The canary population needs care too. If the new path affects a few high-volume tenants, a random one-percent request sample may barely include them, and a targeted cohort is the better test.

Configuration needs this reasoning too. Publishing a new policy revision through the configuration service of Chapter 5 and deploying a new image are different operations, and rolling back one does not roll back the other. The release record therefore names both revisions and their compatibility assumptions. Argo Rollouts can automate the exposure steps, while the evidence that customer outcomes are correct comes from the application’s own business-state checks. That evidence comes from the application’s own business-state checks.

Versioned Deployment Policy Enforcement

Everything so far assumed the release was allowed in the first place. A perfect canary is no help if the change never received approval from someone with the authority to give it. Picture a release that updates the payment integration, raises a database pool limit, and exposes a new checkout flag in a single deployment. Before any of it reaches production, someone has to confirm which image is being deployed, which configuration revision goes with it, whether the migration is compatible, whether the required tests passed, and whether the person approving the deployment is allowed to.

Suppose a validation service checks all of that on Monday and approves image A with configuration revision 17. On Tuesday, a Jenkins job deploys image B, or the policy changes overnight and now forbids the pool limit. If the deployment controller trusts Monday’s approval without checking again, the check and the action have drifted apart. Security engineers call this a time-of-check/time-of-use problem, and the fix is to tie the approval tightly to the thing it approved.

One workable contract issues a short-lived authorization bound to the image digest, the target environment, the configuration revision, the operation identity, and the policy version. The deployment controller checks that binding, and the current revocation list, at the moment it deploys. If the policy service is unavailable, the change waits rather than slipping through on an unchecked approval. Notice where the check lives. It sits in the deployment path itself, because a Slack message saying “approved” informs people but cannot stop a misconfigured Jenkins job.

You do not need a large platform to start. A validation module backed by PostgreSQL covers this design, and separate policy storage, an event broker, or regional replicas can wait until a measured requirement calls for them. Appendix B develops the full system, including its API records, integration delivery, and policy drift.

Summary

The query release passed every check the rollout used, because a deployment process checks only what someone decided to check. Readiness confirmed that new instances started. The regression was in connection occupancy, and no step compared it between the old and new versions.

Treating a release as an experiment fixes that. You write down what the change should improve and what would make you stop, you give a canary the same load as the instances it is compared with, and you decide the gate before the data arrives, so a promising number cannot talk you into promotion. Feature flags separate installing code from activating it. Expand-then-contract migrations make sure the previous version can still read what the new one wrote, and that compatibility makes rollback dependable.

Rollback restores code, while the records and events the new version produced persist. At Baodium, that limit exposed a different kind of coupling. Separate pipelines did not mean independent releases while two teams shared the same database tables, and Chapter 11 starts from the outage that made this visible.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & A query that returns correct results and improves an isolated benchmark also reduces resource use under production concurrency.
Condition that tests it & A new version increases connection occupancy or fails on a subset of instances.
Constraint or invariant & The canary instance receives about 400 lookups per second, the same rate as each stable instance, and promotion requires version-specific evidence measured against criteria recorded before the release.
Evidence and uncertainty & Mean connection occupancy rose from 70 to 85 milliseconds, raising average use from 28 to 34 of 40 connections per instance.

Still unknown: how request mix, placement, cache state, and shared database contention affect the comparison, and what early exposure cannot reveal about full-fleet cost or infrequent operations.
Signal and evaluation window & Version-specific occupancy, acquisition time, errors, and page latency, compared over nonoverlapping five-minute intervals with a minimum sample.
Control and decision & Increase exposure only when the required sample satisfies both relative and absolute criteria, pause for missing evidence, and restore the approved stable path when an abort condition applies. After restoration, verify routing, resource recovery, and user-facing outcomes.
Owner and review trigger & The service owner defines the expected improvement and regression criteria, the release owner manages exposure and unresolved pauses, and data owners approve compatibility transitions and the rollback target. Review after any release that is paused or aborted, and before changing the release policy.
